name: Contact Energy Limited
sector: New Zealand Electricity Gentailer (Integrated Generator-Retailer / Utility)
overview: Contact Energy is New Zealand's second-largest integrated electricity generator and retailer ("gentailer"), generating power from geothermal, hydro, thermal (gas) and, following the 11 July 2025 acquisition of Manawa Energy, an expanded fleet of 30 hydro schemes, while retailing electricity, natural gas, broadband and mobile to c.646,000+ customer connections. Contact is dual-listed on the NZX and ASX and reports in NZD; its FY2025 EBITDAF was $872m (reported) / $774m (underlying) on total revenue of $3,439m, with total generation of 8.9TWh, 97% of which was renewable by 1H FY2026. The business is capital-intensive: it is mid-way through a c.$2bn+ four-year renewable build programme (Tauhara and Te Huka 3 geothermal now online; Te Mihi Stage 2, Kōwhai Park solar and Glenbrook-Ohurua battery under construction) layered on top of the transformative, scrip-and-cash Manawa hydro acquisition.

business_model.summary: Contact makes money two ways that are intentionally linked: (1) Wholesale generation, selling electricity into the NZ wholesale spot market, to Commercial & Industrial (C&I) customers on fixed-price or pass-through contracts, and internally to its own Retail division; and (2) Retail, buying power from its own Wholesale book (and other generators) to sell to mass-market residential/SME customers bundled with gas, broadband and mobile ("multi-product" >149,000 connections). The Wholesale segment is the profit engine (FY25 EBITDAF $994m gross before Unallocated/Retail costs; H1 FY26 Wholesale EBITDAF $577m) while Retail runs at a structural EBITDAF loss/breakeven (H1 FY26 Retail EBITDAF -$25m) reflecting network pass-through costs and competitive customer pricing. Revenue is a mix of recurring/subscription-like retail bills, medium-term fixed-price C&I offtake contracts (increasingly important post-Manawa), and volatile wholesale spot/derivative revenue that Contact actively manages through Contracts for Difference (CfDs) and other hedges — the company describes itself as using 'risk management assets and controls' to smooth hydrology- and gas-driven price volatility. Geothermal and hydro provide low-marginal-cost baseload/flexible renewable generation; the Taranaki Combined Cycle (TCC) gas plant and Ahuroa Gas Storage (AGS) provide thermal peaking/dry-year backup, kept running longer than originally planned (through winter 2025 and into the strategic reserve discussions) due to hydrology and gas scarcity.

revenue_streams.name: Wholesale electricity (net of hedging)
revenue_streams.trend: declining as fixed-price C&I mix rises

revenue_streams.name: Mass market electricity (Retail)
revenue_streams.trend: growing with connections and Manawa consolidation

revenue_streams.name: C&I electricity - fixed price
revenue_streams.trend: growing (Fonterra, NZ Steel, Oji Fibre deals)

revenue_streams.name: C&I electricity - pass through / other / geothermal services

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C mass-market retail (electricity, gas, broadband, mobile) and B2B/C&I (large industrials such as Fonterra, NZ Steel, Oji Fibre Solutions, and the wholesale market itself)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand generation and retail operations; capital raised and some debt issued offshore (AUD medium-term notes, EUR medium-term notes, USPP notes) meaning currency exposure sits on the funding side, not the revenue side

main_competitors: Independent/challenger retailers (Octopus Energy NZ, Flick Electric, Ecotricity, Electric Kiwi)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the 'big four' gentailers that together control roughly 85% of New Zealand generation and c.95% of back-up/firming supply; post-Manawa, Contact is now the largest owner of hydro generation stations by count (30 schemes) though Meridian remains larger by hydro output/installed capacity and is the largest generator overall. Contact is the leading geothermal generator in NZ following the Tauhara and Te Huka 3 additions.

moat_factors.description: Owning generation and retail together lets Contact hedge wholesale price risk internally, self-supply its retail book, and shield mass-market customers from spot volatility — a structural advantage over pure-play retailers that has drawn direct regulatory scrutiny

Geothermal baseload (Tauhara, Te Huka, Wairākei/Te Mihi) plus now geographically diverse hydro (South Island summer-peaking Clyde/Roxburgh plus Manawa's North Island winter-rain-peaking schemes) plus gas peaking (TCC) and growing battery/solar reduces exposure to any single dry-year or fuel-scarcity event

Dual NZX/ASX listing, Green Debt Instrument framework (DNV-assured Sustainable Finance Framework), and access to AUD, EUR and USPP debt markets support a multi-billion dollar capex programme that smaller/independent retailers cannot fund

646,000+ connections across four products (energy, broadband, mobile) with 149,000+ multi-product customers; customer wellbeing initiatives (disconnection fee removal, Good Plans, Fourth Trimester) support retention but do not create hard switching costs in a market with easy retailer-switching

moat_factors.factor: Development pipeline and consented land bank
moat_factors.description: Long-dated consented and near-consented geothermal, solar, wind and battery pipeline gives Contact optionality to keep growing renewable capacity, though consenting delays (Southland Wind Farm decline) show this advantage is not fully within its control

weaknesses: Retail segment is structurally low/negative margin (H1 FY26 Retail EBITDAF -$25m) and highly exposed to rising network/lines charges (~20% increase from April 2025) that must be passed through, creating political/regulatory friction
Heavy reliance on hydrology and, historically, on a declining domestic gas market for firming — FY25 was hit by two historically dry periods and a 20% YoY fall in gas production
Large, still-being-integrated acquisition (Manawa) with provisional purchase price accounting not finalised until FY26 year-end, and $18-20m of one-off transaction/integration costs already booked

Regulatory target: as one of the 'big four,' Contact is directly named in Electricity Authority non-discrimination/mandatory-hedge proposals and in the broader political debate about gentailer structural or operational separation

Capital intensity requires continuous equity/debt funding (NZ$525m equity raise announced Feb 2026) which dilutes existing shareholders and makes the dividend/growth capex balance a constant investor question

growth_drivers: Manawa Energy acquisition (completed 11 July 2025) — 25 hydro schemes plus 75% of King Country Energy (5 more schemes), added 1.3TWh of renewable generation in H1 FY26 alone, provisional goodwill of $349m reflecting expected cost synergies (>80% of announced synergies already secured as of Feb 2026) and portfolio/hydrology diversification benefits

Renewable build programme: $1.2bn of completed projects (Tauhara 174MW/1.45TWh geothermal, Te Huka 3 51MW binary plant) plus $1.1bn under construction (Te Mihi Stage 2 101MW/$712m online Q3 CY2027, Glenbrook-Ohurua 100MW/~200MWh battery online Q1 CY2026, Kōwhai Park 168MWp solar JV with Lightsource bp online Q2 CY2026)

New NZ$525m equity raise (Feb 2026) funding Glenbrook battery 2.0 (200MW, $235m), the Glorit solar JV (150MWac, $305m) and pre-FID drilling for Tauhara 2 geothermal (60-70MW), under an accelerated 'Contact31+' growth strategy

Electrification/demand growth: long-term supply deals with Fonterra (540GWh p.a. at Whareroa by 2028, ~75% new demand), NZ Steel (Electric Arc Furnace) and Oji Fibre Solutions; national demand growth outlook positive with committed/contracted load plus MBIE reference-scenario growth of ~1.3-1.7% CAGR to 2030 and up to +8% total identified growth by 2030
Multi-product cross-sell (broadband, mobile) growing the non-energy EBITDAF base toward the FY27 ambition of tripling non-energy lines-of-business EBITDAF contribution

Long-term gas contracts (Methanex ~6PJ secured, Greymouth/OMV up to 10PJ p.a. to CY2032) and the 10-year Commerce-Commission-authorised Huntly Strategic Energy Reserve (Rankine Unit 2 firming option, to 2035) reducing dry-year/fuel-scarcity tail risk across the whole gentailer sector

Secular tailwind from New Zealand's stated 2050 net-zero commitment and government moves to accelerate renewable consenting (Fast-Track Approvals Act) even as some projects (Southland Wind Farm) have been individually delayed

business.description: FY25 experienced two historically significant dry periods causing spot/futures price spikes; despite post-Manawa diversification (South Island summer-peaking vs North Island winter-rain-peaking hydro), a severe dry sequence remains the single largest swing factor on annual earnings

NZ gas production fell ~20% between calendar 2023 and 2024, deepening fuel scarcity for thermal peaking (TCC) and gas storage (AGS); Contact has had to secure short-term Methanex gas and sign contracts out to 2032 (Greymouth/OMV) to plug the gap, at rising cost

Large industrial loads (aluminium smelting via NZAS/Tiwai Point demand response, pulp/paper, dairy) move total system demand materially — e.g., FY25 saw a 58% drop in Central North Island demand from mill closures — and the broader NZ economy's health affects both C&I offtake and residential collections/hardship exposure

Purchase price allocation still provisional at 31 December 2025 (intangibles, receivables, provisions to be finalised at FY26 year-end); realizing announced cost synergies and combining risk/hydro-management systems carries execution risk, though >80% of synergies were reported secured by Feb 2026

financial.description: Net borrowings roughly doubled year-on-year (carrying value of borrowings $3,165m at 31 Dec 2025 vs $2,149m a year earlier) following Manawa debt assumption ($545m) and a €500m Euro medium-term note issue; Contact needed a further NZ$525m equity raise in Feb 2026 to fund the next wave of growth capex

Diversified funding across NZD retail/capital bonds, AUD medium-term notes, EUR medium-term notes (hedged via cross-currency interest-rate swaps) and USPP notes means refinancing and swap costs are sensitive to global rate and currency movements even though revenue is 100% NZD

financial.risk: Dividend/capex tension for a capital-intensive yield stock
financial.description: Dividends declared have grown (39.0 cps FY25, up 5% YoY; 16 cps H1 FY26 interim) against a backdrop of $363m FY25 growth capex, $1.1bn of projects under construction and further growth capex committed post-equity-raise — dividend growth could plateau or be increasingly scrip-funded (DRP took up ~$73m of the $228m H1 FY26 dividend) if capex intensity stays high

regulatory.description: The EA is formalising new obligations on the 'big four' gentailers effective as early as mid-2026: mandatory minimum trading volumes in a standardised super-peak hedge product, draft non-discrimination Code amendments (due October 2026) preventing gentailers favouring their own retail arms in wholesale dealings, and a review of 'market making' practices in electricity futures — all aimed directly at Contact's integrated model

regulatory.risk: Political pressure for gentailer structural/operational separation
regulatory.description: NZ First, Greens and Labour have all floated breaking up the gentailer model; the OECD's 2026 NZ Economic Survey flagged that if EA reforms don't materially improve investment, competition and affordability, government should re-examine structural solutions; even 'operational separation' (legally distinct generation/retail entities with separate boards) would raise costs and could pressure the valuation multiple

The Southland Wind Farm consent was declined under COVID-19 Fast Track legislation, forcing a costly resubmission under the new Fast-Track Approvals Act — illustrating that renewable project timelines and costs remain hostage to a still-evolving planning regime despite government reform efforts

regulatory.risk: Cross-industry cooperation arrangements draw competition scrutiny
regulatory.description: The Huntly Strategic Energy Reserve arrangement among Genesis, Contact, Meridian and Mercury required Commerce Commission authorisation (granted, 10 years to 2035) — a reminder that inter-gentailer cooperation, even where pro-competitive in intent, faces regulatory gatekeeping

macro.risk: Wholesale price volatility as intermittent renewables scale
macro.description: Management itself flags 'growing seasonal price spreads' and 'increased price volatility as more intermittent generation enters the market' as a medium-term industry challenge, raising the cost of long-term risk management products Contact relies on to smooth retail pricing

macro.risk: NZ economic slowdown / consumer and industrial demand sensitivity
macro.description: Wider economic pressures on households (energy hardship, disconnection trends) and on gas-exposed businesses were explicitly cited by the Chair; a soft NZ economy dampens both retail volumes/collections and C&I demand growth

macro.risk: Rate sensitivity of a capital-intensive, dividend-paying utility
macro.description: As a high-capex, geared, yield-oriented stock, CEN's valuation and cost of capital are sensitive to NZ and global interest-rate moves, both directly (debt service, WACC) and via relative attractiveness of the dividend yield versus bonds/cash

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ electricity demand is forecast to grow modestly but steadily (MBIE reference scenario ~1.3-1.7% CAGR, with committed/contracted new load plus dairy, metals and data-centre demand potentially adding up to ~8% cumulative growth to 2030) as electrification of industrial process heat and transport progresses, even though FY25 actual demand was roughly flat-to-down due to weather and specific industrial closures/fuel scarcity.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — underlying demand is relatively defensive (essential service, mass-market retail) but earnings are highly cyclical/volatile year-to-year based on hydrology (dry vs wet years) and gas availability, which drive spot prices and the mix of low-cost renewable vs higher-cost thermal generation.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high — large, growing debt stack (~$3.2bn carrying value at 31 Dec 2025) funding a multi-billion-dollar capex programme, and equity yield attractiveness versus term deposits/bonds for a dividend-focused shareholder base.
key_input_costs: Domestic natural gas (scarce, rising price, contracted to 2032)
Carbon/emissions costs (NZ ETS carbon price exposure, ~$23-70m annually)
Network/lines transmission and distribution charges (passed through but politically sensitive, up ~20% from April 2025)
Construction/EPC costs for geothermal, solar and battery builds (inflation and supply-chain risk on the $1.1bn+ under-construction programme)

recent_developments.event: H1 FY2026 result: EBITDAF up 24% YoY to $500m, NPAT up 44% (profit $205m attributable, EPS 20.9cps), reflecting first-time consolidation of Manawa Energy; total generation 97% renewable vs 89% prior-year half; interim dividend declared 16 cps, payable 25 March 2026

NZ$525m equity raise announced (NZ$450m institutional placement at $8.75/share, ~7.2% discount, plus up to NZ$75m retail offer) to fund Glenbrook battery 2.0 (200MW/$235m), the Glorit solar JV (150MWac/$305m) and pre-FID Tauhara 2 geothermal drilling under the 'Contact31+' growth strategy
FY2026 EBITDAF guidance updated to ~$965m (up $15m vs prior guidance), with H1 EBITDAF of $500m and unchanged mean-hydro assumption for H2

Commerce Commission granted 10-year authorisation (to 2035) for the four gentailers' Strategic Energy Reserve / Huntly Firming Option, incentivising Genesis to keep Rankine Unit 2 available as dry-year cover for the whole market, including Contact

FY2025 full-year result: underlying EBITDAF $774m (+17%), reported EBITDAF $872m (boosted by a $98m non-cash release of the Ahuroa Gas Storage onerous contract provision), underlying NPAT $261m (+13%), full-year dividend 39.0 cps (+5%); Tauhara (174MW) and Te Huka 3 (51MW) both operating a full year for the first time, geothermal generation +34% to 4.5TWh

Completion of the Manawa Energy acquisition via Scheme of Arrangement — 100% of Manawa's shares acquired for a mix of Contact shares ($1,649m) and cash ($351m); Manawa delisted from NZX 5 August 2025 after early bond redemption; acquired assets include 25 hydro schemes plus 75% of King Country Energy (5 more schemes), $2,568m of PP&E and $545m of assumed borrowings, provisional goodwill $349m

Electricity Authority formalising new rules for the big-four gentailers: mandatory minimum hedge trading volumes in a standardised super-peak product, draft non-discrimination Code amendments due October 2026, and a futures 'market making' review, with implementation targeted mid-2026

Southland Wind Farm consent declined under COVID-19 Fast Track legislation; Contact resubmitted under the new Fast-Track Approvals Act, delaying and adding cost to a project the company says could bring $200m+ to the Southland economy

items.notes: Up $15m from prior guidance; H1 FY26 EBITDAF already $500m (+24% YoY on a Manawa-consolidated basis); H2 assumes mean hydro conditions

items.target: Elevated multi-year programme; incremental $235m (Glenbrook battery 2.0) + $305m (Glorit solar JV) + Tauhara 2 pre-FID drilling funded by the Feb-2026 $525m equity raise, on top of the existing $1.1bn under-construction programme (Te Mihi Stage 2, Glenbrook-Ohurua BESS, Kōwhai Park solar)
items.notes: Accelerated under the 'Contact31+' strategy; FY25 growth capex (cash) was $363m, down 14% YoY as the geothermal wave completed, but reaccelerating with the new battery/solar/geothermal pipeline

items.target: 16 cps interim (H1 FY26), consistent with prior growth trajectory (FY25 full-year 39.0 cps, +5% YoY)
items.notes: Board declared 16 cps interim dividend 13 Feb 2026, payable 25 March 2026; dividend reinvestment plan (DRP) remains active and is absorbing a meaningful share of the cash dividend (~32% of the $228m H1 FY26 total was DRP)

items.target: More than 80% of announced cost synergies secured
items.notes: Provisional purchase price accounting (goodwill $349m) to be finalised at FY2026 year-end

items.metric: FY27 strategic ambitions (Contact26 strategy, set May 2023)
items.target: Facilitate 100MW of new demand; reach 100MW Demand Flex; grow to 10.3TWh p.a. renewable generation; 100MW battery operational; >685k connections; cost-to-serve <$80/connection; triple non-energy EBITDAF contribution; Scope 1&2 emissions run-rate ~300ktCO2e toward 2035 net zero
items.vs_prior: maintained, tracking mostly on-plan with some minor delays (e.g. Southland Wind Farm)
items.notes: Set out in the FY25 Integrated Report as medium-term ambitions under the original Contact26 strategy; company noted in the FY25 Chair's letter that it is undertaking a strategic review to ensure Contact remains well positioned beyond Contact26/into 'Contact31+'

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mike Fuge described H1 FY26 as reflecting effective risk management and the benefit of new geothermal capacity, with Manawa integration ahead of plan on synergies. The Chair's FY25 letter struck a more cautious tone on the operating environment — accelerated gas decline, dry-year hydrology, rising lines charges, and 'increased volatility in the wholesale market' — while reiterating confidence that continued renewable investment, not undefined market restructuring, is the right response, and expressing concern about the potential chilling effect of gentailer break-up rhetoric on investment confidence.

bull_case: Manawa Energy acquisition materially diversifies the hydro fleet (North Island winter-rain vs South Island summer-snowmelt), reducing single dry-year earnings risk while adding scale — H1 FY26 already shows EBITDAF +24% and NPAT +44% with >80% of announced synergies captured ahead of plan

Renewable growth pipeline is large, funded and de-risked: $1.2bn already delivered (Tauhara, Te Huka 3) plus $1.1bn under construction (Te Mihi Stage 2, Glenbrook-Ohurua battery, Kōwhai Park solar) plus a newly funded $540m+ tranche (Glenbrook battery 2.0, Glorit solar JV) backed by a fresh $525m equity raise, positioning Contact to keep growing EBITDAF as low-marginal-cost renewable output replaces higher-cost thermal generation

Structural demand tailwind from electrification — long-term, high-volume fixed-price contracts already signed with Fonterra (540GWh p.a.), NZ Steel and Oji Fibre Solutions, against a national demand backdrop where MBIE and Contact's own analysis point to multi-year demand growth

FY2026 EBITDAF guidance of ~$965m was raised (not cut) at the H1 result, with analyst consensus rating the stock a 'Buy' and a consensus price target (~NZ$10.4) meaningfully above the recent trading price (~NZ$9.10-9.35), implying room for further re-rating as Manawa integration proves out

Reliable, growing dividend (39.0 cps FY25, +5%; 16 cps H1 FY26 interim) with a DRP that partially self-funds the growth programme, appealing to NZ's large yield-seeking retail and KiwiSaver investor base
bear_case: Regulatory risk is rising, not falling: the Electricity Authority is imposing mandatory hedge-trading volumes and non-discrimination obligations on the big-four gentailers from mid-2026, and NZ First, Greens and Labour have all floated structural or operational separation of generation from retail — a genuine tail risk to the vertically integrated model that underpins Contact's margins

Balance sheet has re-levered quickly: carrying value of borrowings roughly doubled to $3.2bn in the 12 months to Dec 2025 (Manawa debt assumption plus new EUR/AUD notes), and Contact needed a further $525m equity raise in Feb 2026, raising the question of how much more dilutive/debt-funded capital the multi-year growth programme (Contact31+) will require

Earnings remain exposed to hydrology and gas scarcity: FY25's underlying result relied partly on a one-off $98m non-cash AGS provision release, and two historically dry periods plus a 20% YoY fall in NZ gas production show the fuel-security backdrop is structurally worsening, not improving, even as Manawa's added hydro diversity helps at the margin

Manawa purchase price allocation and integration is not yet finalised (provisional at 31 Dec 2025), and 'combined' pre-acquisition financials were not disclosed as immaterial — leaving limited visibility into whether the acquired hydro assets are performing to the assumptions used to justify the deal

Retail segment continues to run at a loss/breakeven (H1 FY26 Retail EBITDAF -$25m) with rising network pass-through costs (~20% lines increase from April 2025) creating ongoing political pressure on pricing and headline profitability optics, even though Wholesale more than compensates
